posts.title: Too Topical?
posts.description: SOMETIMES life too much imitates art. As with the case of the U.S. Army’s lead-filled “dirty bomb” due to be detonated in Iowa on November 25, 2026. Tomorrow morning. Three years ago we ran a short story, “Glow Worm Farm,” by Kathy Lanzarotti , which describes the toxic after effects of an explosion in a remarkably similar part of the American landscape. An excellent, moving story, worth reading. At the time we ran it we saw it as a cautionary tale. Speculative. Suddenly it’s become all too real. Is this once-great nation losing its mind? There were plans seven months ago to safely neutralize the toxic lead azide, used as triggers for weaponry. What happened? “Too expensive” was the rationale for not doing so, some claim. Others wonder whether someone somewhere wants the landscape to become contaminated, no longer able to grow crops, in order to allow the construction of giant data centers there. posts.title: About Pop Culture
posts.description: IS POP SATIRE POP LIT? LIKE MANY people and projects, at New Pop Lit we’ve had, from the beginning, a love-hate relationship with pop culture, which at its best is fun, quick and colorful, often with a punchy sense of immediacy. Which has been the pop template at least since the days of the early Beatles, and maybe before that, Elvis Presley. Pop Art pioneered a similar path, with much stress on personality and celebrity. On modernist icons, representatives of our mad commercial civilization where the stance, the pose, the look and style are everything. Pop was used as a way to revive isolated or stagnant art forms: music which became too precious, virtuosic, and slow; or paintings too obscure, inscrutable and bland, fit only for dusty museums overseen by snooty caretakers, in a hidden-dimensional realm at which only pontificating critics could understand. posts.title: Fall Fiction 2026
posts.description: COUPLES AND SINGLES, MEN AND WOMEN Divides and conflicts between men and women seem to be a constant theme in social media of late, and even, on occasion, in the news. How to behave? How to get a person on the “other” side to be more agreeable, as if we’re on competing teams? We have no answers!– though we’re a couple ourselves, one who stumbled together in part through our common love of language and literature. Relationships may be up to fates, angels, or vibes, qualities beyond our conscious minds. Anyway, we have as our new feature a short story which examines the subtleties of human relations, whether one is on the inside or outside. The mysteries of love and life as portrayed in the wonderfully written “Raspberry Leaf” by Paula Brancato . We know you’ll enjoy it.
